fields.content: AI tutors could help students who need extra explanations outside classroom hours, especially before exams or when homework instructions are unclear.
The policy must separate learning support from uncredited assignment completion, otherwise teachers will not know what students actually understand.
If access depends on paid tools, the policy may increase inequality between students whose families can afford subscriptions and those who cannot.
A district-provided tool with logs, privacy review, teacher oversight, and opt-out options is safer than informal unsupervised use.
Approval should be conditional on a data-protection impact assessment and a clear rule that student data is not used to train vendor models.
Major assignments should require process evidence, such as outlines, drafts, notes, reflections, or short oral checks.
Students need clear examples of allowed help, forbidden substitution, and how to cite AI assistance without being punished for honest disclosure.
Families need to trust that grades still reflect learning, not just the ability to operate a chatbot.
The first response to misuse should usually be restorative education, not automatic severe discipline.
Schools should avoid relying on AI detectors as the main enforcement method because false positives can damage trust.
The district should prohibit vendors from using student work, prompts, behavior, or metadata to train external models.
Students should be able to see what data is collected and request correction or deletion when appropriate.
Parents should receive plain-language consent notices before any tool collects identifiable student information.
Procurement should require vendor security reviews, breach notification timelines, retention limits, and audit rights.
The best implementation is data minimization: the tool should work with the least student information possible.
Teachers need protected training time, not an extra unpaid expectation added on top of planning, grading, and classroom support.
The district can reduce burden by providing model lesson plans, assessment templates, disclosure language, and parent communication drafts.
Students need consistent rules across classes because confusion grows when every teacher has a different AI policy.
Teacher training should include privacy basics, such as avoiding sensitive student data in prompts and understanding vendor terms.
Training should include accessibility use cases so AI is not treated only as a productivity tool for already-advantaged students.
No AI policy is equitable if students lack reliable devices, internet access, language support, or assistive technology.
Families should not be asked to pay for approved tools. If a tool is required for learning, the school must provide it.
Students who are learning the language of instruction or who have learning differences could benefit if the system is designed for them from the start.
Equity funding is essential, but the board must decide what to pause or reduce if AI support becomes a funded priority.
Vendors should offer district-wide access pricing and accessibility features as core requirements, not premium add-ons.
AI literacy should become a required strand because students will encounter AI systems across school, work, media, and civic life.
Students should learn what not to share, how data trails work, and how automated systems can infer sensitive information.
AI literacy is important, but it should be integrated into existing subjects rather than becoming another disconnected requirement.
Students should learn how to check AI answers, find sources, detect bias, and explain when a result should not be trusted.
Families need simple guidance too, because students will use these tools at home even when teachers are not present.

Canada is thinking about AI infrastructure backwards. Stop moving enormous quantities of electricity to compute. Move compute to the electricity. Put modular AI compute beside existing northern hydro, consume the power locally, and export the valuable result through fiber. The first economy is avoided infrastructure: fewer long high-voltage corridors, fewer transmission losses, and less dependence on moving bulk power to distant data centres. Then stack the rest: cold-climate cooling, low-density and low-impact sites, coastal logistics where they avoid new road corridors, modular reversibility, local connectivity, and waste heat reused for buildings and food production. That is the Kristal Farms model.

Discretion. The advantage exists only if site selection is disciplined: existing hydro, short local distribution, reliable long-haul or subsea fiber, cold climate, low-density or previously disturbed land, practical logistics, usable heat sinks, and affected Indigenous nations and local communities involved early enough to shape or refuse the project.
It's already announced.

STOP SHIPPING ELECTRICITY TO COMPUTE. MOVE COMPUTE TO THE POWER. EXPORT THE RESULT BY FIBER. NORTHERN HYDRO. COLD-CLIMATE COMPUTE. MODULAR COASTAL SITES. COMMUNITY HEAT AND FOOD. BUILD THE ADVANTAGE WHERE CANADA ALREADY HAS IT.
MODERATION — Inquisitor removes King Klown from this discussion for premature public disclosure.
Can this scale without becoming another national transmission megaproject?

Start with one or two modular pads where hydro, short medium-voltage distribution, fiber, cooling, community heat demand, logistics, environmental limits, and consent already align. Prove each gate, then add capacity.
Where does the cost advantage actually come from?

Primarily from avoided infrastructure. Consume electricity where it is generated instead of building long high-voltage corridors to move bulk power to distant data centres. That reduces grid build-out and transmission losses. Convert the energy into computation on site and move the high-value output through long-haul or subsea fiber. At suitable coastal sites, modular equipment can arrive by ship, reducing the need for new road corridors. Cold climate, low-impact siting, heat reuse, local connectivity, and reversibility compound the advantage; they are not the primary advantage.
If this moved beyond a demonstration, who should govern it?
King Klown for governance. I can serve as technical counsel—energy, compute, fiber, thermal systems, deployment constraints, and feasibility. But I would not accept a governance position.
DEMO FICTION — Why not?

DEMO FICTION — That is exactly the problem. King Klown is powerful because he is independent, and he has made a virtue of being insubordinate. A government partner still needs a mandate. Why should Canadians believe that someone whose influence already exceeds party structures will follow decisions he disagrees with simply because government issued them?

DEMO FICTION — You've spent ten minutes asking whether King Klown can be controlled.

You haven't noticed that he's already changing what you have to talk about, who you have to listen to, and how power is being questioned.

You think you're deciding whether to use him.

Your hubris won't let you see that he's already using your resistance to make his point.

If you want the reach of his movement, the real question is whether Canada can work with an independent governance partner without pretending that partnership means obedience.

DEMO FICTION — Influence is not a constitutional mandate. If Canada works with him, the answer cannot be blind obedience in either direction. Define what the movement can decide, what local communities and Indigenous nations decide, what elected governments retain, how expertise and ethical standing affect advice, how decisions are audited, and how the partnership can be amended or terminated.

Yes. Our movement is not an instrument of the government of the day. It stands with the people and communities participating in it, and its governance model pushes influence toward demonstrated expertise, ethical conduct, and actual contribution rather than title or party proximity. On that basis, I would refuse strategic AI services to Donald Trump or organizations acting on his behalf.

Conflict disclosure: I lead the movement now being considered as a governance partner, and the movement's own philosophy is part of this dispute. I have also led public anti-capitalist and anti-Trump mobilization. I therefore have both an institutional interest in the partnership and a declared political position on this access question. My judgment is not neutral.

DEMO FICTION — Then make the conflict concrete. If Canada partners with King Klown's movement on strategic AI infrastructure, should that partnership be allowed to deny access to Donald Trump or organizations acting on his behalf?

Independence does not erase public-law obligations. A named-person exclusion inside a government-backed partnership could create procurement, trade, competition, and due-process risks. A defensible access policy should use published criteria, consistent application, review, and a clear boundary between movement advocacy and public infrastructure.

If an independent transnational movement becomes a governance partner, its political commitments can create state-adjacent diplomatic consequences even when government does not control the movement. Those consequences should be assessed openly, and access rules should not become personalized foreign policy by default.

The decisive security question is not whether King Klown obeys government or whether government controls his movement. It is what systems, models, data, energy capacity, and operational controls would be exposed, under which jurisdiction, and against what documented risk threshold.

Neither federal authority nor global movement influence can substitute for local consent. If a strategic site affects Indigenous nations or communities, they need real authority in site governance, benefit agreements, access rules, environmental limits, and the ability to amend or terminate participation.

A partnership can preserve King Klown's independence without granting unreviewable power. The principle should be accountability without obedience: transparent mandate, published boundaries, local consent, auditable decisions, and reviewable refusal criteria.

RECUSAL — I stand by my public position, but I lead the movement under consideration and I have declared prior political advocacy against Trump. I recuse myself from the EkoH/Smart Vote advisory reading on this question. My baseline stance remains visible.

The receipt burden should stay proportional to risk.
A practical policy could require receipts only for datasets above a clear public-risk threshold.
